label: copy phase (every output step after the first)
explanation: Broad copy-phase feature: fires on about 97% of copy-phase steps (t > L, recall_idx >= 1), no matter which token is input or output, how long the sequence is, or what token comes first. It is essentially silent in the original phase (about 0.1% of steps, only late positions) and on the <DEL> step (recall_idx 0). Average activation per step is somewhat higher early in the copy phase (recall_idx 1-3) than late, and the top activations peak around recall_idx 1-2. Token identity changes the rate very little.

issues: No systematic counterexample found. On the test split, predicate phase==2 scores P=0.967, R=0.999, F1=0.983, mass recall 0.9997.

Missed activations (2989 test steps, 0.0% of mass) are all weak firings at the last original-phase positions (orig_idx 3-8, mostly at orig_idx 7-8) and on <DEL>. This matches the claim of 'only late positions'.

False positives (about 3.3% of copy steps) are spread evenly. The copy-phase firing rate stays between 0.94 and 0.97 across every slice tried: digit vs letter out_tok (0.958/0.968), in_tok==out_tok (0.962), repeated tokens (prev_tok==in_tok 0.960, next_out==out_tok 0.963, out_count>=2 0.968), recall_idx 4 (0.951), L==3 (0.944), last step to_go==0 (0.958), L9 recall 8 (0.937).

The magnitude claim holds but the effect is small. Mean activation mass per step is about 0.39/0.46/0.37 at recall_idx 1/2/3, versus about 0.29-0.36 later, and the top examples peak at recall_idx 1-2.

Minor point the explanation leaves out: activation magnitude (not firing rate) varies somewhat by output token. For example out_tok x and v carry about 0.055-0.060 of the mass versus about 0.038 for t and q at similar counts. This does not contradict any claim.
The label 'every output step after the first' slightly overstates coverage, since the feature actually fires on 97% of those steps. It is otherwise consistent with the predicate.
